text: Lessons 5 through 7 built an Azure network and VM, then an AWS network and instance, as if they were two separate projects. They don't have to be — this lesson combines both into one real multi-provider configuration, and covers the alias pattern for when one cloud alone needs more than one region.

Declaring azurerm and aws together in the same required_providers block isn't new syntax — it's literally Lesson 5's azurerm block and Lesson 6's aws block, side by side. Terraform doesn't care that one talks to Azure Resource Manager and the other to AWS's APIs; it builds one dependency graph across every resource in the file regardless of provider.

That single graph is the real payoff: one terraform apply provisions resources in both clouds, and one terraform plan shows the full blast radius of a change across both at once — instead of two disconnected projects with two separate applies someone has to coordinate by hand, which is exactly how multi-cloud configs drift out of sync in practice.

A single provider "aws" {} block configures one region, because region can only hold one value per block. The moment a design needs a primary region and a disaster-recovery region, one block isn't enough — the fix is a provider alias: two independent aws configurations, same provider type, same credentials, different region each.

A resource that doesn't set provider = uses the default, unaliased block automatically. One that needs a specific aliased configuration says so explicitly — provider = aws.east or provider = aws.west — which is exactly the shape a real DR design takes: a primary instance and a standby, planned and applied together from one state file, no second Terraform project required.

Every resource from both clouds across this entire chapter now lives in one state file. Chapter 3 opens with exactly the problem that creates: Why Local State Doesn't Scale to a Team, covering what breaks the moment that one file is sitting on a single person's laptop instead of somewhere a whole team can reach.
